details:
**Apep (Apophis), the serpent of chaos**
Ra's archenemy is Apep, a giant serpent of chaos and darkness who lives in the underworld. Every night Apep tries to stop or swallow Ra's boat, sometimes with a hypnotic gaze, and Ra must defeat him so the sun can rise again. Ra is defended by Set, who stands at the prow of the boat and spears the serpent, and by the coiled protector serpent Mehen. In one form, the "Great Cat" of Heliopolis, Ra himself cuts off Apep's head.

**The solar barque: Mandjet and Mesektet**
Ra sails across the sky by day in a boat called the Mandjet ("Boat of Millions of Years"). At sunset he moves into the night boat, the Mesektet, and travels through the Duat (underworld) during the twelve hours of night, rising again in the east each morning.

**Isis learns Ra's secret name**
Ra kept a secret true name that held his power. When he grew old and drooled, Isis mixed his saliva with earth (clay) to make a poisonous snake, which bit him. Only she could cure the poison, and she agreed to do it only if he told her his secret name. With that name she gained great magical power, which she used to benefit her son Horus.

**Sekhmet and the red beer (the Destruction of Mankind)**
In the Book of the Heavenly Cow, humans plotted against the aging Ra, and he sent his Eye, in the form of the goddess Hathor turned into the bloodthirsty lioness Sekhmet, to slaughter them. When he changed his mind, he had seven thousand jars of beer dyed red with ochre (in some versions pomegranate juice) and poured over the fields. Sekhmet drank it, thinking it was blood, became drunk, and stopped, and she became the gentle goddess Hathor again. Ra then withdrew into the sky on the back of the cow goddess Nut, who was held up by Shu and eight Heh gods (the "Infinite Ones").

**The Eye of Ra**
The Eye of Ra is an independent goddess, his violent, protective power, who can take the form of Hathor, Sekhmet, Bastet, Tefnut, or Wadjet. In the myth of the Distant Goddess she leaves Egypt in anger and is coaxed home, in one Demotic version by a baboon telling her fables, including the mouse and the lion. She also appears as the uraeus, the rearing cobra coiled around the sun disk on Ra's head.

**Khepri, Ra, and Atum (Khnum): forms through the day**
Ra appears in different forms during the day. Khepri, a scarab beetle rolling the sun disk the way a dung beetle rolls a ball of dung, is the morning sun. Ra is the sun at midday. Atum, or the ram-headed Khnum, is the sun in the evening as it sinks in the west. Ra is often merged with Atum as Atum-Ra.

**Heliopolis, the Mnevis bull, and the Bennu bird**
Ra's main cult center was Heliopolis (Iunu), home of the Ished tree, a sacred tree of life. The black Mnevis bull worshipped there was considered his living embodiment, and his soul (ba) was linked with the Bennu, a heron-like bird that inspired the Greek phoenix.

**Amun-Ra and Ra-Horakhty**
Ra was merged with many other gods. During the New Kingdom, the Theban god Amun was fused with him as Amun-Ra, king of the gods. Ra-Horakhty ("Ra-Horus of the Two Horizons") combined him with Horus, which is why Ra is usually shown as falcon-headed. The pharaoh Akhenaten pushed aside these cults in favor of the worship of the sun disk, the Aten.

**Nut forbidden to give birth and the five extra days**
Ra forbade the sky goddess Nut from giving birth on any day of the 360-day year. Thoth gambled with the moon god Khonsu (in some versions playing senet) and won enough moonlight to create five extra (epagomenal) days, on which Nut gave birth to Osiris, Isis, Set, Nephthys, and in some lists Horus the Elder.

**Shu and Tefnut, born from spit or a sneeze**
As creator, Ra (as Atum-Ra) produced his first children, Shu (god of air, whose name means "emptiness") and Tefnut (goddess of moisture), by spitting or sneezing them out. They gave birth to Geb (earth) and Nut (sky), making Ra the grandfather of Geb and Nut and the ancestor of the whole Ennead, the nine gods of Heliopolis. In one story he grieved when Shu and Tefnut went missing.

**Humans created from his tears**
Humans were said to have been created from the tears (and sometimes sweat) of Ra; Egyptian words for "tears" and "people" sound alike. Humans were called "the cattle of Ra."

**Rising from the primeval waters of Nun**
In Heliopolitan creation myths, Ra appeared from Nun (Nu), the dark primeval waters of chaos, either on the first mound of land (the benben) or blossoming out of a blue lotus flower. Nun also sometimes acts as his adviser.

**Hathor dances to cheer him up**
In the Contendings of Horus and Seth, Ra was insulted and lay down sulking. His daughter Hathor danced naked (or exposed herself) in front of him and made him laugh, which cheered him up so he returned to judging the case. Ra is also called the father of Ma'at, whose feather is weighed against the hearts of the dead.

**Falcon head, sun disk, and the "Son of Ra"**
Ra is usually shown as a falcon-headed man wearing a sun disk circled by a uraeus cobra. Egyptian pharaohs claimed to be his descendants, and "Son of Ra" became one of the standard royal titles.
